summaries.example: Imagine a student who finds many science books written in a language they cannot read. Falaquera gathered ideas from those books, explained them in Hebrew, and arranged them so more people could study. He sometimes added Jewish examples or connected the ideas to the Torah. His work was like building a clear library path through a very large collection.
summaries.summary: Shem Tov Ibn Falaquera was a Jewish philosopher who lived in the Middle Ages. We do not know many facts about his life, but his books show that he knew a great deal about Greek, Islamic, and Jewish learning. He wanted more of his fellow Jews to study philosophy and science. He wrote in Hebrew and used several kinds of writing: introductions for beginners, collections of earlier teachings, an encyclopedia, a commentary on Maimonides, and explanations of the Bible. Falaquera often used the ideas of Aristotle, al-Farabi, Averroes, Avicenna, and Maimonides. He did not usually try to claim that the ideas were his own. Still, he made important choices about what to include, how to arrange it, and how to connect it with Jewish learning. He taught that philosophy could help people understand the Torah, but that a philosophical teaching that truly disagreed with the Torah should not be accepted. Scholars must study his books carefully because his own opinions may be hidden in the way he combines and changes his sources. His importance comes especially from bringing a wide world of philosophy and science to Hebrew readers.
key_ideas: Falaquera was a thirteenth-century Jewish philosopher and writer who lived probably in Spain, although details of his life are uncertain.
He wanted Jewish readers to learn philosophy and science in Hebrew.
He gathered ideas from Greek, Islamic, and Jewish thinkers and shaped them into books for his readers.
He believed that true philosophy and correctly understood Torah should agree, while a philosophical claim that contradicted Torah should be rejected.
He was not mainly trying to invent brand-new ideas. His creativity often appeared in choosing, joining, shortening, and explaining older sources.
summaries.why_it_matters: Falaquera shows that teaching and organizing knowledge can be important kinds of philosophical work. A person does not have to invent every idea to make a lasting contribution. By translating, explaining, and arranging earlier learning, Falaquera helped connect Greek and Islamic philosophy with Jewish readers and Jewish questions. His writings also show how people can use careful thinking when interpreting religious texts and deciding whether different kinds of knowledge fit together.

important_terms.definition: A person who makes difficult ideas easier for many people to learn.
A shortened explanation made from one or more earlier works.
A large, organized book that gathers knowledge about many subjects.
A careful explanation of a difficult book or passage.
A way of explaining a text, especially Scripture, to discover its meaning.

questions_to_think_about: How can a person make a difficult subject easier without changing its main ideas?
Why might someone place ideas from different books into one new book?
Can a text have both a surface meaning and a deeper meaning?
What should a writer do when two trusted sources seem to disagree?

summaries.example: Suppose a scholar studies several commentaries on the same scientific topic. One is detailed but confusing; another explains a missing point; a third uses a clearer order. If the scholar combines selected passages into a coherent Hebrew account, the result may be more useful than any single source. Falaquera’s work illustrates this method: his originality often lies not in inventing doctrines, but in selection, arrangement, abridgment, translation, and occasional criticism.
summaries.summary: Shem Tov Ibn Falaquera, a thirteenth-century Jewish philosopher probably associated with Spain, is presented in the SEP entry as both a major transmitter of learning and a thinker whose creativity has often been underestimated. His writings aim to educate Jewish readers in philosophy and science and to show that genuine knowledge need not conflict with Torah. He produced an introductory dialogue, the Sefer ha-Mevaqqesh, a trilogy leading readers from moral preparation and the classification of sciences toward Aristotelian natural science and metaphysics, and the De‘ot ha-Filosofim, one of the earliest substantial Hebrew encyclopedias of science and philosophy. Falaquera usually did not simply translate. He selected, abridged, rearranged, blended, and sometimes Judaized Arabic and Greek materials, often without naming every source. This practice could conceal his labor from his readers, but it also enabled him to improve clarity and adapt arguments to his goals. His Moreh ha-Moreh, a partial commentary on Maimonides’ Guide of the Perplexed, is particularly valuable because it identifies Maimonides’ philosophical sources, retranslates passages, and occasionally speaks in Falaquera’s own voice. As an exegete, Falaquera held that Torah teaches truth and that philosophy can uncover meanings not immediately apparent, including metaphorical or hidden meanings. Yet he also maintained that a philosophical claim contradicting Torah must be rejected. The entry characterizes him broadly as a moderate Maimonidean, while noting that scholars must distinguish his own views from the views of authors he transmits. The problem of creation illustrates this caution: his popular works appear to affirm creation from nothing, whereas the Moreh ha-Moreh presents a more technical position in15F
key_ideas: Falaquera’s biography is reconstructed mainly from his writings, so his birthplace, chronology, and some claims about his works remain uncertain.
His central educational project was to make philosophy and science available to Hebrew readers and to defend their study as compatible with Jewish law and belief for intellectually prepared students.
He used multiple literary forms: dialogue, popular tale, paraphrase, encyclopedia, commentary, and biblical interpretation.
His adaptations of al-Farabi, Avicenna, Averroes, Aristotle, and other authorities were selective. He sometimes omitted or reshaped claims that did not serve his religious and educational aims.
The De‘ot ha-Filosofim is especially important as an early, extensive Hebrew encyclopedia of Aristotelian science and philosophy; its clarity could result from combining several commentaries.
His Moreh ha-Moreh reveals more of his own critical voice and examines Maimonides’ sources, while also sometimes disagreeing with Maimonides or the cited authorities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Falaquera matters to the history of philosophy because intellectual transmission is not merely mechanical copying. His Hebrew works opened access to Greek and Islamic philosophy for readers who did not know Arabic, while his combinations and alterations shaped how those traditions entered Jewish thought. He also provides a case study in the relationship among translation, interpretation, religious authority, and philosophical argument. Studying him requires attention to genre and method: a popular dialogue, an encyclopedia, and a scholarly commentary may present different levels of disclosure about an author’s own beliefs.

important_terms.definition: A medieval philosophical tradition associated especially with Aristotle and later Greek- and Arabic-speaking thinkers.
A restatement or shortened rendering of a source that may adjust its order, emphasis, or wording.
A systematic work that gathers and organizes knowledge across a broad field.
A scholarly explanation of a major text, often examining its sources and arguments.
Interpretive study of Scripture, including literal, metaphorical, and deeper readings.
The view that God and the world are related through creation from matter that is eternal, rather than creation from absolute nothingness.
A Maimonidean approach that seeks agreement between the Torah and sound philosophy while allowing philosophical interpretation of difficult passages.

questions_to_think_about: When does arranging and adapting existing arguments become an original intellectual contribution?
How might a writer’s intended audience affect which claims from a source are translated or omitted?
Why would knowledge of a philosopher’s sources change our interpretation of that philosopher’s work?
How does Falaquera’s treatment of Scripture balance literal, metaphorical, and philosophically informed interpretation?
What might explain the difference between Falaquera’s popular statements about creation and his more technical discussion in the Moreh ha-Moreh?

summaries.example: Think of a school club that wants to teach a difficult topic using five books. One member chooses the clearest parts, puts them in a new order, adds explanations, and removes ideas that would confuse the club’s purpose. The final guide is not a simple copy, even if most of its information came from the books. Falaquera worked in a similar way when he brought philosophy and science into Hebrew.
summaries.summary: Shem Tov Ibn Falaquera was a Jewish philosopher and writer from the thirteenth century. The entry knows little about his personal life, but his writings reveal a scholar who had studied a very wide range of Greek, Islamic, and Jewish thought. His main goal seems to have been educational: he wanted Jewish readers to see the value of philosophy and science and to gain access to them in Hebrew. He also believed these subjects could help readers understand the Torah correctly. Falaquera wrote for different kinds of readers. In the Iggeret ha-Vikkuah, a scholar debates a religious person who worries that philosophy is dangerous. In other works, Falaquera guides a seeker toward wisdom, explains how the sciences are classified, and gathers natural science and metaphysics into an encyclopedia. He often worked by paraphrasing earlier authors instead of translating every word. He selected passages, shortened them, joined materials from different books, and sometimes added Jewish references. This means that he was not simply a passive copier. His choices could make an argument clearer or change its emphasis. His commentary on Maimonides’ Guide of the Perplexed is especially important because it studies the sources behind Maimonides’ ideas and sometimes lets Falaquera disagree with them. In interpreting Scripture, Falaquera allowed literal, metaphorical, and deeper readings. He held that sound philosophy and the true meaning of Torah agree, but that a philosophical claim opposing Torah must be rejected. The entry therefore presents him as a careful transmitter and an inventive organizer whose own views must be separated from the views he reports.
key_ideas: Falaquera lived in the thirteenth century, probably in Spain, but the evidence about his life is limited.
He hoped to encourage Jewish readers to study philosophy and science rather than treating them as forbidden or irrelevant.
His books brought together Greek, Islamic, and Jewish sources, especially ideas linked with Aristotle, al-Farabi, Averroes, Avicenna, and Maimonides.
His writing took many forms, including a debate, a story about a seeker, a science encyclopedia, and a commentary on Maimonides.
Falaquera often changed the order or wording of his sources and sometimes added biblical or rabbinic material so that the works fit his educational and religious goals.
He thought philosophy could help explain difficult parts of the Torah, but he did not accept a philosophical teaching that conflicted with Torah.
summaries.why_it_matters: Falaquera helps us understand how ideas travel between cultures and languages. His work connected Greek and Islamic philosophy with medieval Jewish readers, but it also shows that translation can involve judgment. Choosing what to include, how to explain it, and which religious questions to emphasize can shape a whole tradition of learning. His writings are also a useful reminder that an author’s opinions may appear not only in direct statements, but in the structure and selection of the material they present.

important_terms.definition: A writer who spreads complicated knowledge to a wider audience by explaining and organizing it.
A shortened or reshaped version of an earlier text that keeps its main subject while changing its presentation.
A book that organizes knowledge about many areas into one connected work.
An explanation of a difficult work that discusses its meaning, sources, and arguments.
The interpretation of a sacred or important text, sometimes looking for meanings beyond the most obvious reading.
A philosophy influenced by Aristotle, whose works shaped much medieval Jewish and Islamic thinking.

questions_to_think_about: Is a person being original if they create something new by combining older ideas?
Why might Falaquera have wanted to write in Hebrew instead of leaving the material in Arabic?
What are the advantages and risks of using a dialogue to teach philosophy?
Why might a writer give different explanations of a difficult topic in beginner and advanced books?
How can readers tell which ideas belong to an author and which ideas come from the sources they use?
